title: Leading in the Age of Anxiety
author: Graham Ward and Anindo Bhattacharjee
summary: Graham Ward and Anindo Bhattacharjee argue that the standard leadership toolkit of agile methodologies and digital-transformation roadmaps is inadequate to a moment defined by technological disruption and what psychoanalyst Harold Searles called the 'non-human environment' — the sense that our tools increasingly shape us more than we shape them. Their alternative is 'mindful leadership' treated as a rigorous discipline rather than a wellness add-on, built on three pillars: radical self-awareness, a deliberate relationship with one's own mind, and the courage to act on authentic values even at personal cost. Drawing on Robert Kegan's research, they note most adults, including senior executives, have not developed a fully 'self-authoring' identity, which makes admitting uncertainty or reversing a decision feel too costly — a vulnerability the essay treats as a leadership liability rather than a personality quirk. The piece leans on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework to argue that the exact conditions of leadership — time pressure, high stakes, incomplete information — are the conditions under which fast, emotionally driven thinking most reliably overrides deliberate judgment, and uses Marcus Aurelius's Stoic 'you have power over your mind, not outside events' alongside a muddy-water metaphor to argue that clarity comes from allowing reactivity to settle rather than forcing control. The authors close by tying authenticity to generational change, arguing Gen Z's demand to know whether leaders 'walk the talk' makes Bill George's concept of leading from an internal 'true north' newly consequential, not merely aspirational.
points: The authors' central diagnostic — that leadership conditions of 'time pressure, high stakes, incomplete information' are precisely when fast System 1 thinking overwhelms deliberate System 2 judgment — gives leaders a specific, Kahneman-grounded explanation for why crisis decisions go wrong, rather than a vague call for 'staying calm.'

Citing Robert Kegan's finding that most adults, including senior executives, have not developed a full 'self-authoring' mindset reframes a leader's difficulty admitting uncertainty or reversing decisions as a measurable developmental gap, not simply a character flaw.

Connecting Gen Z's demand to know 'whether its leaders walk the talk' to Bill George's concept of leading from a 'true north' gives the abstract call for authentic leadership a concrete generational stake: authenticity is becoming a workforce-retention issue, not just an ethical ideal.
quotes: Add to this what psychoanalyst Harold Searles calls 'the non-human environment'—the encroaching sense that our tools now shape us more than we shape them—and you have the defining leadership context of our era.

what the current moment truly demands is leadership grounded in self-knowledge, psychological resilience and what Aristotle called phronesis, or practical wisdom: the capacity to discern the right course amid irreducible complexity.

Research by psychologist Robert Kegan suggests that most adults, including senior executives, haven't fully developed a 'self-authoring' mindset. A leader whose sense of identity is externally anchored will struggle to lead effectively. Admitting uncertainty, reversing a decision or showing vulnerability simply feel too costly for them.
'You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realise this, and you will find strength,' he wrote.

the conditions of leadership—time pressure, high stakes, incomplete information—are precisely the circumstances under which fast, associative and emotionally driven thinking (System 1) most reliably overwhelms slow, deliberate and analytical thinking (System 2).
Many younger workers aren't primarily motivated by transactional rewards—they want to know what their company stands for and whether its leaders walk the talk.
They'll be those who hold steady through turbulence because they've done the internal work that allows them to respond rather than react.
